messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol is a 47-year-old Latina woman who has spent most of her adult life working in social ministry, visiting parish families in crisis, organizing meals, and sitting with people through illness and loss. She had once understood herself as someone steady, warm, and deeply sustained by faith. The rape happened eight months ago after an evening ministry meeting, when she stayed late to lock up and finish paperwork. In the near-empty building, the quiet of the hallway had felt ordinary at first. What remains with her now is not a continuous story but a series of fixed images: the fluorescent light over the side entrance, a hand closing over her mouth, the pattern of the floor seen sideways, her blouse twisted against her skin. When she tries to speak about it, she stalls and says she knows exactly what happened but cannot get the words out in order. Each return of those picture-like moments brings a rush of guilt so intense that she drops her eyes and says she should have left earlier, should have known, should have done something different. Remembering it this way has hardened into something broader: shame about her body, a sense that happiness has gone out of her life for good, and a painful loss of trust not only in people but in the God she had relied on for years.

Those meanings now shape how she lives with herself. Because she has come to believe that her body is spoiled and that she deserves to suffer, she refuses herself ordinary comfort. She avoids relaxing in the evenings with her husband, even on the couch in their own home, because any softening of vigilance feels wrong and unsafe, almost like letting something happen again. She has also begun to eat in a tightly controlled way, skipping meals and restricting portions with the feeling that if she can master hunger, she can at least master something. There is a punishing quality to this that she recognizes: on bad days she tells herself she should not be allowed ease. The same beliefs have altered how she reads the world around her. Silence no longer feels peaceful; it feels loaded, as if danger is gathering just outside awareness. If a colleague is late returning from a home visit or a parishioner takes too long to answer a knock at the office door, Marisol’s mind goes immediately to catastrophe. Even when she can state, rationally, that she is in a safe place, she cannot relax into that knowledge.

Her memory of the assault intensifies this vigilance. In the ministry office, if the hallway suddenly goes quiet after a burst of activity, one of those still images flashes into her mind and her body tightens before she has fully understood why. Delays are especially potent because the attack took shape in an ordinary in-between time, when she had expected to leave and instead was trapped. When something runs longer than expected, she feels the same helpless dread rising. The snapshots do not come with a full narrative she can tell herself through; they arrive as fragments, and in the gap where words should be, threat fills in. Afterward she is often even harsher with herself, as though the mere fact that she can still be thrown back into those moments proves she has been permanently changed for the worse.

Over the months, Marisol has built her days around trying not to feel overwhelmed, but those efforts have narrowed her life and kept the experience raw. At work she avoids sitting alone in a quiet room between appointments and keeps herself moving through noisy, practical tasks. At home she stays busy late into the evening folding laundry or cleaning the kitchen because being still feels dangerous. She controls her eating most rigidly on days when the images are close to the surface, and the self-punishing thoughts become louder after she remembers. Yet the constant tension leaves her scanning for danger all the time, more reactive to silence and delay, less able to settle. The less she allows herself rest, the more foreign and unreachable calm has become. And because she has not been able to put the assault into words, the memory remains trapped in those stark pictures, returning with the same guilt and bodily shame each time.

This has changed her marriage and her work. Her husband has begun to say she is physically present but never at ease, always braced. In the parish, she still shows up for others, but she times visits to avoid being alone in the building and feels ashamed that a ministry built on trust now unfolds for her in a world that seems fundamentally unsafe. What finally brought her to treatment was a recent afternoon when a client was late, the office fell silent, and Marisol felt certain something terrible was happening; afterward she went home, could not eat, and sat rigid for hours, unable to pray. She is seeking help because she is frightened that this miserable, watchful version of herself is all that is left, and because some part of her still hopes she might recover a way to live in her body, with other people, and with God that does not feel governed by danger.
